content: The history of medicine in Canada originates from the oral traditions of the First Nations people. However, with the arrival of English and French settlers, the medical system became dominated by military surgeons and Western medical practices. In the 18th century, Dr. David Parker, practicing in the Maritimes, became the first physician to perform surgery using anaesthesia. Another significant milestone was achieved by William Fraser Tolmie in British Columbia, who conducted one of the first modern surgical procedures by successfully removing a tumour. During the 19th century, the establishment of medical schools began in Upper Canada in the 1820s. Among these was the Montreal Medical Institution, which later became the Faculty of Medicine at McGill University. In the mid-1870s, Sir William Osler revolutionized medical education in the Western world by introducing a hands-on, practical approach to medical training. The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Upper Canada was founded in 1839 and became permanently incorporated in 1869. The 19th century also saw significant progress in the inclusion of women in medicine. Female physicians Emily Howard Stowe and Jennie Kidd Trout successfully fought for the right of women to attend medical schools and obtain licenses from the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario in 1871. In 1883, Emily Stowe spearheaded the establishment of the Ontario Medical College for Women, which was affiliated with the University of Toronto. In 1892, Dr. William Osler authored The Principles and Practice of Medicine, a seminal textbook that shaped medical education in the Western world for the next four decades. The 20th century brought groundbreaking discoveries and advancements in Canadian medicine. In 1922, Frederick Banting, along with Charles Best and J.J.R. Macleod, discovered insulin, a life-saving treatment for diabetes. In 1934, Dr. Wilder Penfield developed the Montreal procedure, a surgical technique for treating epilepsy, and founded the Montreal Neurological Institute, which became a leading center for neurological research and treatment.
